Ops AI by Chanl AI · Architecture and install guide

Ops AI architecture and installation guide

This guide is for the architects, DBAs, security reviewers and operators of a team that runs Ops AI on its own infrastructure. It says what each part does, how work moves through them, where data is kept and how it is kept apart, how the platform is secured, how to deploy and run it, and which parts are built today and which are still to come.

Each status in this guide is read from the code of the release it ships with. Built means it runs and is tested; Partial means some of it runs and the rest is named; Planned means designed and not yet in the code.

Runs on PostgreSQL 15 or newer Install with one script: git clone, then ./install.sh Docker Compose on Linux (x86-64 or ARM64), or Kubernetes Sign-in with OIDC, SAML or password Azure SQL: scripts ready for review, services not yet Team isolation inside the database: in progress

1Overview

What Ops AI does

Ops AI is an operational AI platform. A bank's or other regulated business's operations teams use it to hand routine back-office work to software: reading a court notice and opening a case, triaging a complaint email, placing a hold on an account, answering a staff question from the team's own procedures. A person approves anything that moves money or changes a record in another system, and every step leaves a record an auditor can read.

It runs on your own infrastructure, against a database your DBA controls and a model endpoint you choose. Nothing calls home.

In three parts

Agents

a configured model with instructions, tools, knowledge, skills and guardrails. It decides its own next step inside the limits it was given. People reach it through chat, other systems through the API.

Workflows

a versioned graph of typed steps that runs the same way every time and journals each step. It survives a crash without repeating a write, and waits days for a person at no cost.

Shared services and gateways

reviews and human tasks, cases, knowledge, files, documents, identity and audit, used by both. Every call to your systems leaves through the data gateway, every model call through the AI gateway.

Who uses it

PersonWhat they do in Ops AI
Operations staffChat with the team's agents, open cases, answer the tasks a workflow hands them
ReviewerApproves or rejects what an agent or a workflow wants to write, with a fresh sign-in for payments
Operations managerOwns a process: its cases, its waiting tasks, its cost
BuilderConfigures agents, workflows, tools, knowledge bases and document types, and publishes them through a review
Security adminControls which hosts the platform may call, the stored credentials, storage and sign-in
OperatorInstalls, upgrades, backs up and watches the platform

The platform in one picture

Ideas the design rests on

IdeaWhat it means for you
Agents and workflows are two ways of running workAn agent decides its own next step inside the limits it was given. A workflow runs fixed steps and survives a crash without repeating a write. Each works without the other, and they meet only through their public APIs: a workflow step can call an agent, and an agent can start a published workflow as a tool
A person approves every writeA write to one of your systems needs an approval token bound to the exact input the reviewer saw. Changing one character of the input after approval voids it
Two gateways are the only way outTool calls go through the data gateway, which checks the approval, the policy and an allow-list of hosts. Model calls go through the AI gateway, which checks the caller's key, budget and the data's sensitivity
Use cases are configurationA new process is workflows, document types, agents, tools and settings that a builder configures and publishes. No use case needs new code or a new screen. The court order notice used in this guide is one worked example among several
A team is the data boundaryAgents, workflows, knowledge and the work they produce belong to a team. Roles decide what a person may do inside the teams they belong to
Every change is versioned and reviewedAgents, workflows, skills, guardrails, task types and tool modules are published as immutable versions through a review by a second person. A running case keeps the version it started on

2System components

Ops AI ships as eleven long-running containers and one one-shot job. Seven are Python services built from one base image, plus the workflow worker (the agents image with another command), the web console, a policy engine (Open Policy Agent) and one entry point (Caddy). PostgreSQL is yours and runs outside them. Kubernetes runs the same images as the same workloads.

Every image runs as a non-root user (uid 10001). The seven Python images share one base layer of about 626 MB; the console image is about 440 MB.

Rules every service follows

RuleConsequence
A service reads only its own tablesEach service has its own database login and its own migration history. Data from another service comes through that service's API
Calls between services carry a signed service tokenEach service signs with its own key and is trusted only for the calls it is allowed to make. A service holds only the keys it uses
Every request is authenticatedEach service checks the caller's token against platform-service's published keys, so a request that skips the proxy is still refused
Every service refuses a schema behind itA service whose database has not been upgraded to its version stops at start and says which upgrade is missing
Settings come from the environment or a secrets fileAny setting may be a file under /run/secrets named after it. No image holds a secret

Not in the containers

ItemState
The databaseYours: PostgreSQL 15 or newer, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL 16 or newer. Azure SQL is in Azure SQL
A malware scannerThe files service has a hook a scanner calls back on, and a built-in test engine that recognises only the EICAR test file. A production scanner is yours to connect
The app that serves chat widgets on your other sitesPlanned as its own image. Widgets are configured and published in the console today
One process with no container runtimePlanned The services already run together in one process inside an all-in-one image, which the release package does not include

3How work flows

Three flows cover most of what Ops AI does: a person chats with an agent that wants to change something, a workflow pauses for a person and resumes days later, and an email becomes cases that people decide. In each one the same three rules hold: a write waits for an approval bound to its exact input, every outside call leaves through a gateway, and a run's state is saved after every step so a crash or a restart loses nothing.

A chat turn with a tool approval

A member of the operations team asks the team's agent to place a hold on an account. Reading is free; the hold is a write, so the agent drafts it and a person approves it before anything reaches the core system.

StepWhat protects it
The messageThe person's sign-in token names the tenant and team; nothing in the message can change them
The model callThe AI gateway checks the agent's key, its budget and the data's sensitivity before it calls your model endpoint
The pauseThe approval waits in the conversation with its state saved; closing the browser loses nothing
The writeThe data gateway refuses a call whose input differs from what was approved by a single character, a token past its 15 minutes, or a token from a run that another process has since taken over
A repeatA retried call with the same idempotency key returns the first result and writes nothing

A workflow run with a human task

A workflow starts from an API call, an email or an event from another service. The worker runs its steps in order and saves each one. When a step needs a person, the run pauses and holds no worker; the person's decision puts it back on the queue.

SituationWhat happens
A worker dies mid-stepIts lease expires after 15 seconds. Another worker takes the run, raises the lease generation, and continues from the last saved step. A write the first worker already made is found by its key and not made again; anything the first worker sends afterwards is refused as stale
The task's deadline passesThe task shows as overdue, or, when the step says so, the run leaves on its timeout path, for example to escalate. A timeout never approves anything
A step fails three timesThe run fails with the error on its record, and its case shows the failure to people
The workflow is republished mid-runThe run keeps the version it started on; new runs take the new version

Email to case: a court order notice

This is one worked example. A team connects its mailbox, publishes three workflows through review, and from then on each notice a court or tax authority emails, ordering the bank to hold or pay a customer's funds, is read, checked, turned into cases and answered. Nothing in it is code written for court orders: the document type, the workflows, the tools and the task types are configuration.

ConfigurationWhat it holds
The mailboxProvider, folder, the credential's name in the credential store, and the address replies come from
A document type, "court order notice"The fields to read, their checks, the score floor, and the examples corrections have taught it
Three workflowsMailed documents (one run per message), Mailed document (one per attachment), Court order case (one per debtor)
ToolsSearch customers, list accounts, place hold, add a note, send a reply: operations on your systems with their approval policies
Task typesCheck the read, hold or flag, send the acknowledgement: what the person sees and the actions they can take

Other worked examples in the release use the same parts: complaint email triage, a hold requested through the API, and a customer summary built from the core system and an agent.

4Data and database

Ops AI keeps everything in one PostgreSQL database. Each of the seven services owns its own tables, applies its own migration history and connects with its own login, which can read and write rows in that service's tables and nothing else. File bytes live outside the database, on a volume or in object storage.

Tenants and teams

A tenant is your installation's organisation; a team is the data boundary inside it. Roles decide what a person may do inside a team; they never open another team's data.

5Security and governance

Ops AI is built so that software can draft any change and only a person can let one through. The controls below are layered: who you are (sign-in), what you may do in a team (roles), what a single write needs (approvals), where a call may go (the gateways and the allow-list), and what is kept as evidence (audit).

Sign-in and SSO

MethodHow it worksStatus
OIDC single sign-onAuthorization code flow with PKCE (S256); asymmetric signing algorithms only; the issuer is pinned. Works with any OIDC provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, configured as a generic OIDC providerBuilt
SAML 2.0 single sign-onService-provider-initiated; signed responses required, signed requests and encrypted assertions supportedBuilt
Which provider a person usesChosen by their email domain, once the domain is proven with a DNS TXT recordBuilt
Multi-factor authenticationThrough your identity providerBuilt (by the provider)
PasswordFor an installation with no identity provider: PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations, at least 12 characters, a lockout after 5 failures in 15 minutes, reset links by mailBuilt
Fresh sign-in for sensitive decisions (step-up)A payment approval needs a sign-in less than five minutes old, by password or through the same identity provider; the decision keeps a fingerprint of itBuilt
InvitesAn admin invites by email; the invite holds a hashed single-use token; a person who already has an account signs in firstBuilt

Sessions: platform-service signs a short-lived access token (Ed25519, 15 minutes) and renews it with a rotating refresh token for a session of 8 hours. A reused refresh token is refused and recorded in the audit log. Every service checks tokens itself against platform-service's published public keys.

Roles

A person holds a role in each team they belong to. A role is a grid of 19 areas (agents, workflows, tools, secrets and egress, files, documents, reviews, cases, settings, access, audit and others) by 8 actions (view, create, edit, publish, delete, run, decide, manage). Every check in every service goes through that grid; no code checks a role's name.

RoleWhat it may do in the team
AdminEverything in the team. Actions reserved for the Security team still need a role there
BuilderReads the team's work; creates, edits, tests and publishes its agents, workflows, tools and knowledge
ReviewerReads the team's work and decides its reviews and tasks; in the Security team, decides tool module security reviews
ViewerReads the team's work and chats with its agents
Security adminChanges the outbound allow-list, credentials and storage for every team, and decides tool module security reviews
Chat userChats with the team's agents

The six built-in roles, seeded per tenant, and the grid behind themBuilt
A page that shows each role's grid and why an action is refusedBuilt

The tool gateway

Every call to one of your systems, read or write, goes through the tools service. Agents and workflows hold no credentials and open no connections of their own.

ControlWhat holdsStatus
RegistryOperations come from tool modules: imported from OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1, discovered from an MCP server, or written by a builder. A module's major change opens a Security review; calls keep the published shape until the new version is publishedBuilt
ConnectionsHow the platform signs in to a system, per test and production: API key, basic or bearer, OAuth client credentials, OAuth authorization code with PKCE, client certificate (mutual TLS). Tokens are stored encrypted and refreshed one at a timeBuilt
Each person signing in to a system with their own accountA run would use only the token of the person it acts forPlanned
Test and productionLive runs and chats call production; tests call the test environment, and writes in a test always answer from the operation's mockBuilt
Outbound allow-listHTTPS only, to hosts on your tenant's list. Every address a host resolves to is checked inside the connection, so DNS cannot be used to redirect a call. Private ranges are allowed only when listed; loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses never. No redirects are followed and no cookies kept. The list starts empty: nothing is reachable until a Security admin adds a hostBuilt
Your internal certificate authorityTrusted for outbound calls when you provide its certificateBuilt

Code toolsTransforms and formulas run in a bounded child process with no network or files; no general code runtimePartial

Audit and evidence

Every security-relevant change and every call to the outside is recorded: the audit log, the tool call log, the credential, allow-list, connection and storage audits, the run journal, each review decision and the model call log. Details and status are in Data and database.

Platform hardening

ItemWhat holds
NetworkOnly the entry point publishes a port. On Kubernetes, a network policy admits platform-service's private port only from the other services
ContainersNon-root (uid 10001). On Kubernetes: every capability dropped, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem except the console, the runtime's default seccomp profile
DatabaseOne login per service with row rights on its own tables only; no running container can change the schema when your DBA applies it
Service callsEach service signs its calls with its own Ed25519 key, and a callee accepts only the calls that caller is allowed to make
Policy engineThe gateway writes its policy into the policy engine at start and reports unhealthy if the engine serves a different one; token expiry is judged by the gateway's clock
TelemetryNone. Nothing in the platform calls home

6Models

Every model call in Ops AI, from an agent's turn, a workflow's AI step or a document read, goes through one internal service: the AI gateway (models-service). It knows which key is calling, what that key may still spend, which model a name points at, and how sensitive the data is that the model may receive. Services hold a model key; none holds your provider's credential.

Aliases

An alias is a name such as default that agents, workflows and document types use instead of a provider's model id. Each alias has versions; the newest current version serves. A version names the provider connection, the provider's model, its price per million input and output tokens, the highest data sensitivity it is cleared for, and whether it may receive images and files. Moving an alias to another model is a new version; no agent changes.

ItemStatus
OpenAI-compatible endpoints: any provider or private gateway that serves the OpenAI chat completions API, streamed or not, with tool callsBuilt
Chat and embedding aliases, versioned, with prices and clearanceBuilt
Binding an alias at install with the connect-model commandBuilt
Anthropic's own API as a providerPlanned a connection can be registered, but the gateway does not serve it yet
Failover between providersPlanned

Budget per tenant on a shared keyA tenant's share of a key's budget, refused with tenant_budget_exhaustedBuilt

Data sensitivity

Each alias version is cleared for a level: public, internal, confidential or restricted. A call may name the level of the data it carries, and the gateway refuses it when the alias is not cleared for that level. Images and file parts are refused by an alias not cleared for them, and every call records how many it carried.

ItemStatus
The gateway's check of a call's level against the alias's clearanceBuilt
Callers marking each call with the level of its dataPlanned today every call is treated as internal, so an alias must be cleared for internal to serve
Page images for document reads only where the document type, the team's policy and the alias all allow themBuilt

The test model

The release package includes a stand-in model endpoint that speaks the same OpenAI-compatible API and answers from fixed rules: plain text, or a tool call when a rule matches the message. It calls no provider and costs nothing. Use it to try the platform before your model endpoint is ready, and for automated checks; it is not for production. The automated use cases of each release run on it, so no real model call is made in testing.

7Deployment options

The same images run in every layout. What changes is how they are started, how secrets reach them and where the bytes of files are kept. PostgreSQL is always yours, outside the containers.

OptionShapeStatus
One machine with Docker Compose./install.sh from a clone: every container on one Linux machine, one published port behind your TLS terminator, images pulled from ghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai or loaded from the offline image file. A second machine with the same install is a standby you restore a backup ontoBuilt proven on one machine by the install script's proof
KubernetesKustomize: a base with one folder per service and an overlay per environment, applied with kubectl apply -k. A migrate Job, one Secret per service, a network policy, an outside PostgreSQLBuilt proven on a local kind cluster; not yet on a managed cloud cluster
A Helm chartPlanned the Kustomize overlays carry the same choices
One VM with no container runtimeThe services as host processes under systemd, with native PostgreSQLPlanned

Single-tenant and multi-tenant

ChoiceWhat it meansStatus
One installation per organisationThe install creates one tenant, its Security team and the first admin. Departments are teams inside it, and the team is the data boundary between themBuilt the recommended shape
Several organisations in one installationEvery row carries its tenant, and the agents and platform tables enforce it in the database. Creating a second tenant, per-tenant model aliases and keys, and tenant policies in the database for every service are still to comePlanned

The network

DirectionFromToPortWhy
InboundYour TLS terminator or load balancerThe proxyOPS_PUBLIC_PORT (8890 by default), plain HTTP inside your networkThe console and the APIs, all on one origin
OutboundThe servicesPostgreSQL5432, TLS where the server requires itAll data
OutboundmodelsYour model endpoint443Model calls
OutboundtoolsYour systems443, hosts on the allow-list onlyTool calls
Outboundworker and toolsYour mail server or mail API993 for IMAP, 587 or 465 for SMTP, 443 for Microsoft Graph or GmailTeam mailboxes and replies
OutboundplatformYour identity provider443Single sign-on, key discovery
OutboundplatformYour DNS resolvers53Proving an email domain for single sign-on
OutboundfilesS3 or Azure Blob, when configured443File bytes
Outboundthe hostghcr.io (or your own registry), unless images are loaded from the offline image file443Install and upgrade only

Nothing else needs to leave your network. Put TLS in front of the proxy: the containers speak plain HTTP to each other on the private network.

Sizing

PartStarting pointNotes
One machine for Compose4 vCPUs, 8 GB memory, 60 GB disk to start; any current 64-bit Linux on x86-64 or ARM64 with Docker Engine 24 or newer and Compose 2.22 or newer. The install script's preflight wants at least 4 GB of memory for the containers and 15 GB of free diskIn the release's install proof all containers together used about 2 GB of memory at rest. Images take about 1.2 GB of disk
PostgreSQL15 or newer; on Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, 16 or newer. General Purpose, 2 vCores, 8 GB memory, 64 GB storage to startDatabase size grows with open work and with history until retention jobs exist. No extensions are needed
Kubernetes requests50m CPU each; memory 256 MiB, 512 MiB for agents, worker, documents and console, 128 MiB for the proxy (requests equal limits)One replica each. files and kb keep bytes on a 1 GiB ReadWriteOnce volume each, so they run one replica; raise the size for real use
Workflow throughputEach worker process runs 4 runs at once and polls every half secondAdd worker processes to add capacity; a run waiting for a person holds no worker
File storageThe size of the documents and attachments you keep, for as long as their retention class saysMove to S3 or Azure Blob for large volumes and WORM retention

Load figures for many concurrent runs are still to be measured and published; size against a pilot of your own workload and watch the work queue and database load (Operate).

8Install

One script installs Ops AI on a machine with Docker from a clone of the repository, asks a few questions, checks the result, and later upgrades, backs up, restores and reports on the same install (Operate). It pulls the published images by default; a release's offline image file, or a build from source, serves a machine with no registry access.

The published images are at ghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai.

Before you start

ItemWhat you needDetails
A hostOne Linux machine with Docker Engine 24 or newer, Docker Compose 2.22 or newer, curl and tar, 4 GB of memory for the containers and 15 GB of free diskSizing
A DNS name and TLSA name such as ops.example.com on your load balancer or reverse proxy, forwarding to the port the script asks forThe network
PostgreSQLFor a trial, the script's built-in database. For real use, your own PostgreSQL 15 or newer: either a login that may change the schema, or DBA mode, where your DBA applies the scripts the install writesData and database
A model endpointAny OpenAI-compatible endpoint and its key; the built-in test model will do for a first lookModels
The first adminA name and email address for the person who signs in first and invites everyone else
Sign-in and outbound hostsYour identity provider's OIDC or SAML details, and the hosts Ops AI will call, for the Security admin to set after the installSecurity and governance

Install

git clone https://github.com/chanl-ai/ops-ai.git
cd ops-ai
./install.sh

The host needs Docker 24 or newer, Docker Compose 2.22 or newer, curl, tar, 4 GB of memory for containers and 15 GB of free disk. Python is not needed: the steps that use it run inside the images. The preflight names anything missing and stops.

It asks these questions. Each has a default, a flag, and a key for an answers file (--answers <file>, one KEY=value per line), so CI can run it unattended with --yes.

QuestionDefaultFlagAnswers key
Port on this machine8890--portPORT
Public URLhttp://localhost:<port>--public-urlPUBLIC_URL
Compose project nameops-ai--projectPROJECT
Organisation nameMy organisation--orgORG_NAME
First admin's email and nameadmin@example.com, First Admin--admin-email, --admin-nameADMIN_EMAIL, ADMIN_NAME
First admin's password (12+ characters)generated, kept in ops-ai.env--admin-password-fileADMIN_PASSWORD
Databasebuiltin: a PostgreSQL 17 container, for a trial--database builtin or --database postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbDATABASE
Database mode (own PostgreSQL only)auto: the migrate job applies the schema with the given login--db-mode auto or --db-mode dbaDB_MODE
Modeltest: the built-in test model--model test or --model <OpenAI-compatible base URL>/v1 with --model-name and --model-key-fileMODEL, MODEL_NAME, MODEL_API_KEY
Image versionthe checkout's version tag, else deploy/release/version--versionVERSION

What it does, in order:

  1. Pulls ghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai/<image>:<version> (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). --build builds them from the checkout's HEAD instead; --offline <images.tar.gz> loads a release package's image file.
  2. Writes ops-ai.env (mode 600) from deploy/compose/app.env.example and generates every key with the platform image's generate_keys.py. No secret is printed.
  3. In dba mode, copies the release's PostgreSQL scripts to ./dba/postgres (from the db-scripts image), writes ./dba/1-server.sql with each service login's password, prints three psql commands for the DBA, waits, and checks each service's schema version before going on. The DBA runs them as the server admin; the schema is owned by ops_migrator, and no container gets a login that may change it.
  4. Starts the database, migrations and services, connects the model, then starts the agents, worker, console and proxy, waiting for every health check. A provider key is stored in Secrets through the API as MODEL_PROVIDER_KEY, never in ops-ai.env; models-service reads it by that name.
  5. Runs the check: health through the published port, the console's sign-in page, a sign-in as the first admin, one read from every service through the proxy, and agents' health (a model is connected). Then it prints the URL and how to sign in.

Running ./install.sh again on a working install checks it, says "nothing changed" and changes nothing. On an install that is not running, it reuses ops-ai.env and its keys and starts it. It never makes new keys over existing ones: OPS_SECRETS_KEY unlocks the stored credentials.

The other commands

CommandWhat it does
./install.sh statusVersion, image source, database and model; each container's state; the check
./install.sh logs [service]The last 200 lines, followed on a terminal
./install.sh backup [--out DIR]One .tar.gz in ./backups/ (mode 600): a pg_dump of the database, the files and knowledge volumes, and ops-ai.env
./install.sh restore <file>Stops the services, recreates the database from the dump, puts the volumes back, starts and checks. Refuses a backup made with another OPS_SECRETS_KEY
./install.sh upgrade [--version V]At the same version: checks and changes nothing. Otherwise: backs up, gets the new images, applies the schema (auto) or writes ./dba/upgrade-<from>-to-<to>/ for the DBA and waits, restarts, checks, and on a failed check restores the backup on the old version
./install.sh uninstallAsks, then removes the containers; asks again before deleting the volumes. Keeps ops-ai.env

In dba mode, backup, restore and upgrade need an admin login that may dump the database, given as a file: --admin-url-file <file holding postgresql://admin:password@host:5432/db>. A runtime login cannot dump it (row-level security); without the file the script stops and says to ask the DBA.

ClaimEvidence
Clone to signed in, images pulled from GHCRinstall_proof.sh steps 1 to 3, run with SIGNED_IN=1 (a registry login) while the packages are internal; the anonymous run waits for them to be public (unverified)
Every console page loadsdocs/usecases/lib/stg_click_walk.mjs, steps 4 and 7
A rerun and a same-version upgrade change nothingsteps 5 and 6: ops-ai.env checksum and container ids unchanged
Backup and restorestep 7: a table and a file made after the backup are gone after the restore

Images and the version: deploy/release/version names the version a checkout installs. A version tag v<version> runs .github/workflows/release-images.yml, which builds every image for both platforms with deploy/release/images.sh and pushes <version> and latest. The same script builds the release package's images (release-package.md) and --build.

By hand

Every step the script runs can also be run by hand: the Compose files and settings in Ops AI on Docker Compose, the DBA's scripts in The database, and a Kubernetes install in Ops AI on Kubernetes.

9Operate

How to check, upgrade, back up, restore and scale an Ops AI install. The install script's commands come first; the manual commands after them are the fallback, and the ones Kubernetes uses.

Run the script's commands from the clone the install ran in; they read its settings from ops-ai.env there. In the manual commands, $C is the Compose command for your install, for example docker compose -p ops-ai -f deploy/compose/app.yaml -f deploy/compose/dba.yaml --env-file ops-ai.env, and ops-ai is the Kubernetes namespace.

Status and health

CheckWith the scriptBy hand: ComposeBy hand: KubernetesHealthy
Everything at once./install.sh status: version, image source, database and model, each container's state, then the install's checkThe check passes
Every container$C pskubectl -n ops-ai get podsEach service Up (healthy) or Running and ready; the migrate job exited 0
The entry pointcurl -fsS https://<your host>/api/platform/v1/healthSame{"status":"ok"}
Sign-inOpen your address and sign inThe console opens
ServiceHealth routeWhat it proves
platform/v1/healthProcess up
agents/healthProcess up, database reachable, and a model connected: it answers 503 until one is
workera database queryProcess up and database reachable
tools/healthProcess up, and the policy engine serves the gateway's own policy: it answers 503 policy_drift otherwise
models, kb, files, documents/healthProcess up
console/loginThe console serves
proxy/api/platform/v1/healthThe proxy reaches platform

Logs

TaskWith the scriptBy hand: ComposeBy hand: Kubernetes
One service./install.sh logs agents: the last 200 lines, followed on a terminal$C logs -f agentskubectl -n ops-ai logs deploy/agents -f
Every service./install.sh logs$C logs --since 1hkubectl -n ops-ai logs deploy/<service> --since 1h
The schema job./install.sh logs migrate$C logs migratekubectl -n ops-ai logs job/migrate

Every service writes plain text lines to standard output, one event per line with key=value fields, for your log collector to pick up. Structured JSON output is planned.

Upgrade and roll back

./install.sh upgrade --version <new version>

At the same version it checks and changes nothing. Otherwise it backs up, gets the new images, applies the schema (or, in DBA mode, writes the upgrade scripts to ./dba/ and waits for your DBA), restarts, checks, and on a failed check restores the backup on the old version. In DBA mode it needs an admin login that may dump the database, as a file: --admin-url-file <file>.

By hand, and on Kubernetes:

StepWhoWhat
1DBABack up the database (below)
2OperatorGet the new release's images
3DBAApply the new release's database upgrade script as the schema owner, then its grants script. Each step checks the version it starts from and stops before any change when the database is somewhere else
4OperatorStart the new images. Every service checks the database's schema version and refuses to start on one older than itself
FactConsequence
A service refuses a schema it does not knowAn older release cannot start on a newer schema, so two releases cannot be mixed by mistake
Migrations do not roll back on their ownTo go back, restore the backup from before the upgrade, or run the release's downgrade script where every step has one, and start the previous images
An index added to a very large table holds writes while it buildsThe upgrade script names such indexes; on a table over about a million rows, build the index by hand first with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and the upgrade then finds it
A drift check compares a live database with what its release expectsIt lists every missing, extra or changed object
Runs in flight keep their versionA waiting run resumes on the new release with the workflow or agent version it started on
The script has not yet upgraded across two releases that change the schemaThe first release has no earlier one to upgrade from

Back up and restore

./install.sh backup
./install.sh restore backups/<file>.tar.gz

A backup is one .tar.gz in ./backups/, readable only by its owner: a dump of the database, the files and knowledge volumes, and ops-ai.env. A restore stops the services, recreates the database from the dump, puts the volumes back, starts and checks; it refuses a backup made with another OPS_SECRETS_KEY. In DBA mode both need --admin-url-file <file>, since a service's login cannot dump the database under its tenant policies.

A backup holds ops-ai.env and its keys. Keep it as safe as the database: OPS_SECRETS_KEY unlocks every stored credential, and without it a restored installation cannot call your systems.

By hand, back up the database with your usual PostgreSQL tools, or on Azure with the automated backups and point-in-time restore. Back up as the server admin: the tenant policies apply to the schema's owner too, so pg_dump as the schema owner stops with a row-level security error.

docker run --rm -e PGPASSWORD=<admin password> -v "$PWD/backup:/backup" postgres:17 \
  pg_dump -Fc -f /backup/ops.dump "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=ops sslmode=require"
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_files-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/out" alpine tar czf /out/files-data.tgz -C /data .
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_kb-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/out" alpine tar czf /out/kb-data.tgz -C /data .

To restore by hand into a new database:

$C stop
psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=postgres sslmode=require" -c "CREATE DATABASE ops_restored OWNER ops_migrator"
docker run --rm -e PGPASSWORD=<admin password> -v "$PWD/backup:/backup" postgres:17 \
  pg_restore --exit-on-error -d "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=ops_restored sslmode=require" /backup/ops.dump
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_files-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/in" alpine sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /in/files-data.tgz -C /data"
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_kb-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/in" alpine sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /in/kb-data.tgz -C /data"

Then point each service's database setting at ops_restored and start everything again. On Kubernetes, back up the files and kb volumes with your cluster's volume snapshots. When files are stored in S3 or Azure Blob, use that store's own versioning or replication.

Remove

./install.sh uninstall asks, then removes the containers, and asks again before deleting the volumes. It keeps ops-ai.env.

files and kbTheir bytes are on a volume one replica can write, so they run one replica eachPartial

SignalWhy it mattersHealthy
The work queueRows waiting to be claimed mean the workers are busy or downClaimed within a second or two

Rotating keys

KeySteps
Approval key (OPS_REVIEW_KEY)Set the new value for agents and tools and restart both. Approvals in flight must be given again
A service's signing keyGive the service a new key and key id, add its public key to every other service's trusted list beside the old one, restart the others, then the service; then remove the old key id and restart the others again
Sign-in token key (OPS_PLATFORM_SIGNING_KEY)Set a new key and key id and restart every service; people may need to sign in again
Secrets key (OPS_SECRETS_KEY)Changing it makes every stored credential unreadable, so each must be entered again. A rotation that re-encrypts them is planned
A provider's model keyThe Security admin replaces it in the credential store; no restart
Database passwordsChange each login's password, update its setting, restart that service

10Azure SQL

Ops AI does not run on Azure SQL Database or SQL Server yet. The scripts below are ready for your DBA to review now, so the review can run in parallel with the remaining work. Install on PostgreSQL today; Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server is supported.

Azure SQL Database and SQL Server 2025 or later are the second supported database in the design. The services reach the database only through each service's store layer, and the places where the two databases differ (locking, queue claims, inserts that update an existing row, the clock, the tenant of a transaction) sit in one dialect layer, so the services above the stores do not change.

Ready for review

ItemWhat it holdsStatus
roles.sqlRun in master as a server administrator: one SQL login per service plus the schema owner ops_migrator, each password a sqlcmd variable; the database with collation Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8 and READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON, owned by ops_migratorBuilt
One script per service, and bundle.sqlEvery table, index, key and default, the version table stamped at the release, and a security policy per tenant table. The bundle refuses a database with another collation, without read-committed snapshot, or below compatibility level 160Built
grants.sqlA database user per service login with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on its own tables and nothing else; the one system user the background loops switch to, which only the agents login may impersonate, with the same narrow grants as on PostgreSQLBuilt
manifest.json and SHA256SUMSThe commit, each service's schema version, every file's checksumBuilt
Tenant isolationA security policy on each tenant table of the agents and platform services: a filter predicate on reads and block predicates after insert and after update, reading the tenant from SESSION_CONTEXT, which the services set and clear per transactionBuilt in the scripts
Data typesText as VARCHAR(max) under the UTF-8 collation, JSON as NVARCHAR(max), timestamps as DATETIMEOFFSET, booleans as BIT, keys named as on PostgreSQL so later upgrades name the same objectsBuilt
Upgrade scriptsGenerated per release pair the same way as for PostgreSQL, each step guarded by the version it starts fromBuilt
How the scripts are kept rightCompiled from each service's table definitions, which tests hold equal to what the PostgreSQL migrations build, and compared on every change with reviewed copiesBuilt

Your DBA runs them with sqlcmd -b, which stops at the first error:

sqlcmd -b -d master -i roles.sql -v database=ops ops_migrator_password=<...> ops_agents_runtime_password=<...>
sqlcmd -b -U ops_migrator -d ops -i bundle.sql
sqlcmd -b -U ops_migrator -d ops -i grants.sql

Saved run state for workflows and chatsIts three tables are written with PostgreSQL-specific code and are not in the SQL Server scriptsPlanned
Knowledge searchPostgreSQL full-text search has no SQL Server equivalent in the scripts yetPlanned
Sign-in dataThe platform service still sets the tenant with PostgreSQL statements and uses four lookup functions that run before the tenant is knownPlanned
